about: Four harder practice questions per concept (a new situation, why it happens, telling it apart, or working something out), added beside the four easier ones the question generator wrote. Each review asks one easier and one harder question per concept. None of them gives away an answer to the concept's Remem Test. Applied by backend.practice_upgrade.

Origin of Hangul.stem: Which pair of years is right for Hangul?
A historian finds a Korean letter written in 1430. Which script is it most likely written in?
Which statement is supported by the notes?
options: Hangul was created under King Sejong the Great
Hangul was banned by King Sejong

Origin of Hangul.stem: About how many years after Hangul was announced did the year 1500 come?

Hangul Structure.stem: A word is written in 3 syllable blocks. What is the smallest number of letters it can contain?
Hangul has only 24 basic letters. How can it write thousands of different syllables?
options: Each letter has a thousand shapes
Letters combine in many ways inside syllable blocks

Hangul Structure.stem: Which is NOT true about the basic Hangul letters?
options: There are more vowels than consonants

Hangul Structure.stem: A learner knows all the basic consonants. How many more basic letters must they learn to know all 24?

Functions of the Silent ㅇ.stem: In 강, what sound ends the syllable?
Which syllable contains a silent ㅇ?
Why is 가 never written with ㅇ in front of it?
options: ㅇ is only used in names
ㅇ would make it sound like ng
Blocks can hold only two letters
It already starts with a consonant sound, ㄱ

Double Consonants.stem: How many double consonants do the notes list?
Which letter is NOT a double consonant?
How does 싸 differ from 사 in sound?
options: Its s is said tighter and stronger
It has a puff of breath

Double Consonants.stem: Which pair are both double consonants?

Aperture and Depth of Field.stem: A group photo has people standing at very different distances. Which aperture keeps them all sharp?
Which f-number lets in the least light?
A product photo has the whole watch sharp but is too dark. Which change brightens it without changing the depth of field?
options: Raise the ISO or use a slower shutter speed

Aperture and Depth of Field.stem: Which list goes from the widest to the narrowest aperture?

Shutter Speed and Motion.stem: Which shutter speed is best for a sharp photo of a running dog?
A night photo of a road shows long streaks of car lights. What does that tell you about the shutter speed?
Which shutter speed lets the most light reach the sensor?
You change from 1/250 to 1/1000 second. To keep the same brightness, what could you do?

ISO and Image Noise.stem: Two photos of a night street: one at ISO 400, one at ISO 6400, all else the same. Which is brighter?
In a dim gym you need a fast shutter and your lens is already at its widest aperture. What is left to brighten the photo?
Why can a photo taken at ISO 3200 in a dark room still look bright?
options: The sensor is made more sensitive to light

Exposure Balancing.stem: You raise the ISO from 200 to 400. To keep the same exposure, what could you change?
options: Use a wider aperture by one stop
Use a narrower aperture by one stop

Exposure Balancing.stem: Why can't you simply use the fastest shutter speed for every photo?
options: Less light reaches the sensor, so the photo darkens unless something else changes

Exposure Balancing.stem: Which pair of changes keeps the exposure the same?
options: A one-stop faster shutter and a one-stop wider aperture
A faster shutter and a narrower aperture
A lower ISO and a narrower aperture
A slower shutter and a higher ISO

Exposure Balancing.stem: Compared with 1/125 second, how many stops less light does 1/500 second let in?

Composition and Light.stem: A portrait places the person's eyes where two dividing lines cross. Which idea is this?
Why do many photographers avoid shooting landscapes at noon?
options: The light is harsher than the soft, warm light of golden hour
The rule of thirds cannot be used

Composition and Light.stem: To divide a frame into thirds both ways, how many lines do you need in all?
Which placement breaks the rule of thirds?
options: A tree on the left third line
A face where two lines cross
A horizon on the lower third line
A small boat exactly in the centre of an empty sea
Currency tenge, language Kazakh, has the steppe
Currency som, language Uzbek, has Samarkand
Currency somoni, language Tajik, has the Pamirs
Currency manat, language Turkmen, has the Karakum

Uzbekistan's Geography and Culture.stem: A traveller wants to see ancient Silk Road cities and pay in som. Which country fits?
Which statement about Uzbekistan is FALSE?
options: Part of the Aral Sea is there

Uzbekistan's Geography and Culture.stem: Which language is spoken in the country where Bukhara is?

Tajikistan's Geography and Language.stem: What is the capital of the country where the Pamir Mountains are?
Tajik is closely related to Persian. Which other fact in the notes also points to Persian influence in the region?
options: The region was part of the Soviet Union
The ending -stan comes from a Persian word
Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country

Tajikistan's Geography and Language.stem: Which is NOT true of Tajikistan?
options: Its language is close to Persian

Tajikistan's Geography and Language.stem: About what share of Tajikistan is NOT mountainous?

Turkmenistan's Features.stem: What is the capital of the country with the Karakum Desert?
About how much of Turkmenistan is NOT covered by the Karakum Desert?
Which is NOT true of Turkmenistan?
options: It has the Darvaza gas crater

Turkmenistan's Features.stem: Which language is spoken in the country whose capital is Ashgabat?

Confirmation bias.stem: Kiran believes he is weak at maths, so he notices every mistake and ignores the questions he got right. Which bias is this?
A researcher only runs tests that could support her theory, never ones that could disprove it. What is the risk?
options: She may keep a wrong theory because evidence against it is never collected
She will anchor on the first result

Confirmation bias.stem: Which of these is confirmation bias rather than anchoring?
options: Thinking a price is fair because of the first price you heard
Fearing planes after a crash in the news
Searching only for reviews that praise the phone you already chose
Finishing a course because of the fees paid

Confirmation bias.stem: Two friends read the same mixed news about a cricket team. One remembers only the good parts, the other only the bad. What does this show?
options: Each remembers what supports what they already believe
One of them has a better memory

Sunk cost fallacy.stem: Meena has queued for an hour and learns the wait is two more hours. She stays because 'I've already waited an hour'. Which bias is this?
Why is money already spent called 'sunk'?
options: It was spent on something useless
It cannot be got back whatever you decide next

Sunk cost fallacy.stem: A student has paid for a coaching course that turns out to be unhelpful. Which thought shows the sunk cost fallacy?
options: I'll compare it with free resources
I'll stop if it won't help me from now on
I've paid so much, I must finish it
I'll ask whether next month will help

Sunk cost fallacy.stem: Which of these is the sunk cost fallacy rather than framing?
options: Staying in a dull job only because of the years already spent there
Preferring '95 percent fat-free' to '5 percent fat'
Judging a price by the first number heard
Remembering only news that agrees with you

Availability heuristic.stem: After two burglaries in her area were on the news, Lata thinks burglaries are very common. Which idea explains this?
Which of these is the availability heuristic rather than confirmation bias?
options: Remembering only facts that support your view
Thinking floods are common right after one was on the news
Trusting the first price you see
Staying in a course you paid for

Availability heuristic.stem: A doctor who recently treated three rare cases starts expecting that illness in every patient. Which idea explains this?
Why can heavy news coverage make a rare danger feel common?
options: Vivid stories are easy to recall, so they feel frequent
Dangers become common after being reported

Dunning-Kruger effect.stem: After reading one article on investing, Sameer is sure he can beat professional investors. Which effect is this?
As someone gains real skill in an area, what does the Dunning-Kruger idea suggest happens?
options: They become better at seeing their own mistakes

Dunning-Kruger effect.stem: Which of these is the Dunning-Kruger effect rather than confirmation bias?
options: Reading only news that agrees with you
A beginner rating his own skill far too high

Dunning-Kruger effect.stem: Neel scored lowest in his class, yet he guessed he was in the top half. What best explains the gap?
options: He did not care about the test
He anchored on his last score
Low skill made it hard for him to see his own mistakes

Framing effect.stem: A charity says 'Your gift saves 200 lives' rather than 'Without your gift, 200 people will die'. Which effect is it using?
To judge two offers fairly despite framing, what should you do?
options: Pick the one that sounds more positive
Rewrite both in the same terms and compare the numbers
Choose the first one you saw
Ask which one is more popular

Framing effect.stem: Which of these is framing rather than anchoring?
options: Judging a price against the first number you heard
Thinking a sale price is cheap because of the old price
Preferring '80 percent lean' meat to '20 percent fat' meat
Naming the first number in a deal

Framing effect.stem: Which wording is a loss frame for the same train data?

GPS Receiver Functionality.stem: Which part of the GPS system works out where you are?
options: Your receiver, from the satellites' signals

GPS Receiver Functionality.stem: If the United States switched off GPS, which could still give a phone its position, according to the notes?
A receiver knows when a signal was sent and when it arrived. What can it work out from that?
Why does a receiver need signals from several satellites rather than one?
options: One satellite's signal is too weak
One satellite is always behind the Earth
One distance only places you somewhere on a sphere around that satellite

Necessity of Four Satellites.stem: Why can't a receiver with only three satellites fix its own clock error?
options: It needs one more measurement for a fourth unknown

Necessity of Four Satellites.stem: How many unknowns does a receiver solve for, and so at least how many satellites does it need?
Which clock is more accurate: a GPS satellite's or a phone's?
If a receiver had a perfect atomic clock, how many satellites would it need for a position?

Relativistic Clock Corrections.stem: Whose theory describes the effect that GPS satellite clocks must be corrected for?
Engineers build the relativity correction into the satellite clocks. What does that mean for your phone?
options: It must correct for relativity itself
It does not need to correct for relativity itself

Relativistic Clock Corrections.stem: Which of these is a relativity effect rather than a receiver-clock error?
options: A phone's cheap clock being slightly off
Satellite clocks running about 38 microseconds a day fast

Relativistic Clock Corrections.stem: A satellite clock and a ground clock start together. After one day with no correction, which shows the later time, and by about how much?
options: The satellite clock, by about 38 microseconds
The ground clock, by about 38 microseconds
The satellite clock, by about 38 seconds

Navigation Systems and Accuracy.stem: Which list matches each system to its owner?
options: GLONASS: China, Galileo: Russia, BeiDou: European Union
GLONASS: Russia, Galileo: European Union, BeiDou: China
GLONASS: European Union, Galileo: China, BeiDou: Russia
GLONASS: Russia, Galileo: China, BeiDou: European Union

Navigation Systems and Accuracy.stem: A runner's watch shows about 5 metres of error in an open park. What does that tell you?
options: That is normal accuracy under open sky

Serving Size.stem: A 250 g pack lists 12 g of fat per 100 g. How much fat is in the whole pack?
A label gives values per serving, but you eat half a serving. What should you do with the numbers?
A pack holds 2.5 servings of 160 kcal each. How many kcal are in the whole pack?
Which labels let you compare two cereals fairly without any maths?
options: Both given per serving of different sizes
One per serving, one per pack
Both given per pack of different sizes

Percent Daily Value.stem: A soup gives 30 percent of the daily value of sodium per serving. How is its sodium described?
Two servings of a snack each give 3 percent of the daily value of fat. How is the total from both described?
Which of these snacks is low in saturated fat?
options: One with 4 percent of the daily value

Percent Daily Value.stem: Breakfast gives 12 percent and lunch 15 percent of the daily value of fibre. What share is still needed to reach 100 percent?
